questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How families can save money when shopping for food
Why prices are rising and how to control it
How banks decide which people can borrow money
Why Venezuela decided to change its currency
questions.why: Rob and Beth discuss inflation, what is causing price rises and how economists say it can be controlled.

questions.q: What have Rob and Beth both noticed recently?
options: They are both earning much more money than before
Shops are selling fewer products than they used to
Banks are lending money to people more easily
Their money doesn't buy as much as before
questions.why: Beth says our money doesn't seem to buy so much these days, and Rob agrees.

questions.q: Which two things are increasing in price the most?
options: Energy and food
Houses and cars
Clothes and holidays
Food and medicine
questions.why: Beth says energy, like gas and electricity, and food are the two things rising in particular.

questions.q: What two main causes of the price rises are mentioned?
options: Higher wages for workers and lower taxes
Very bad weather and a lot of poor harvests
The Covid pandemic and the war in Ukraine
Rising interest rates and a long recession
questions.why: Rob says the two main reasons are the Covid pandemic and the war in Ukraine, which reduced supply.

questions.q: Why does Linda Yueh think the situation is 'extremely worrying'?
options: Food and energy prices will never come down again
Companies are closing down all over the world
People have stopped buying goods and services
Firms are raising prices, so inflation may stay
questions.why: She says price rises are being passed into how companies price goods, so inflation could stay 'in the system'.

questions.q: According to Linda Yueh, where is inflation most worrying?
options: In advanced economies
In developing countries
In countries with lots of oil and gas
In countries that grow their own food
questions.why: She says it is worrying for advanced economies but 'hugely worrying' for developing countries.

questions.q: What does Vicky Pryce say is the most effective way to control inflation?
options: Slowing demand by raising interest rates
Making banks lend more money to businesses
Cutting the prices of food and energy by law
Printing more money so people can spend more
questions.why: She says slowing down demand is most effective, and higher interest rates discourage borrowing.

questions.q: How does Beth feel after hearing about interest rates?
options: She thinks the idea will not work in practice
She is still very confused about inflation
She finally understands how it works
She is angry about paying more money to banks
questions.why: Beth explains that borrowing less means buying fewer things and says, 'I think it makes sense now!'
